hero.title: Sleep Diary Template
hero.lead:
A sleep diary is a daily record of when you slept, how you slept, and how the following day went. It is unglamorous, takes about two minutes each morning, and it is the single most useful thing you can bring to a doctor about your sleep — because memory is a terrible witness. Lying awake distorts time badly, and almost everyone misjudges how long they were actually asleep.

Here's a template you can copy straight into a notebook or spreadsheet, exactly what to fill in, why two weeks is the number clinicians ask for, and how a diary gets used alongside a sleep study.

sections.heading: The template
sections.html:
One row per night, filled in the next morning. This layout covers everything a clinician needs and nothing they don't:

DateTo bedLights outAsleep by (est.)Wake-upsFinal wakeOut of bedTime sleptQuality 1–5NapsNotes
Mon 8/322:4023:1023:452 (~25 min)06:2006:356h 10m2—Coffee 4pm, wine with dinner
Tue 8/423:0023:0523:201 (~5 min)06:3006:357h 05m4—Gym 18:00, felt sharp all day
Wed 8/500:1500:2001:103 (~40 min)06:2506:504h 35m120 min, 15:00Deadline, mind racing
           

If that's more columns than you'll realistically keep up with, cut it down. A diary with five columns that you complete for fourteen days beats an eleven-column one you abandon on day four. The non-negotiables are lights out, final wake time, and a quality rating.

sections.heading: What to record each morning
sections.html:
Fill it in within the first half hour of getting up, before the night blurs. Taking each column in turn:

  • To bed vs lights out — two different times, and the gap between them is diagnostic on its own. Forty minutes of reading or scrolling in bed every night is a finding.
  • Asleep by (estimate) — your best guess, and a guess is fine. Nobody knows the exact minute they fell asleep, and clinicians expect an estimate. The pattern across two weeks is what counts.
  • Wake-ups — how many, and roughly how long you were awake in total. "3 (~40 min)" is enough detail.
  • Final wake and out of bed — also two different times. A long gap between waking and rising is one of the habits that keeps insomnia alive; see insomnia causes.
  • Time slept — time in bed minus the time you were awake in it. This is the number that gets averaged.
  • Quality 1–5 — how restored you felt, not how long you slept. Subjective is the point.
  • Naps — length and time of day. Long or late naps quietly reduce the following night's sleep pressure.
  • Notes — the column where the answers hide. Caffeine after midday, alcohol, exercise and when, medication, shift work, travel, illness, pain, stress, and how sleepy you were the next day (a simple 1–5 works). Record symptoms too: morning headache, dry mouth, snoring your partner mentioned, bathroom trips.

One important rule: don't clock-watch. Checking the time repeatedly during the night makes both your sleep and your diary worse. Turn the clock away, estimate in the morning, and accept that the estimate is approximate — that is exactly how clinicians read it.

sections.heading: The two-week rule
sections.html:
Fourteen consecutive nights is the standard ask, and there are good reasons for it rather than a round number.

  • Single nights are noise. Everyone has bad nights. A pattern needs enough nights to separate signal from a stressful Tuesday.
  • It captures both weekdays and weekends, twice. The gap between your weekday and weekend schedule — social jetlag — is one of the most common and most fixable findings a diary produces, and you can't see it in five nights.
  • It covers a full cycle of the things that move sleep: work rhythm, exercise, alcohol, travel, and for some people the menstrual cycle's second half.
  • It gives a baseline. Once you change something — a fixed wake time, a CPAP machine, cutting evening alcohol — you need a credible "before" to compare against, and two weeks is enough to be one.

Include the bad nights. A diary edited to look respectable is worse than no diary, because it sends your clinician down the wrong path. Missed a morning? Leave the row blank rather than reconstructing it three days later — a gap is honest data, an invented row isn't.

At the end of the fortnight, work out three numbers: average time slept, average time in bed, and your sleep efficiency (time asleep divided by time in bed, as a percentage). Efficiency above roughly 85% is generally considered healthy; a much lower figure usually means you're spending too long in bed for the sleep you're getting, which is the exact pattern behavioral treatment targets.

sections.heading: How clinicians use a sleep diary
sections.html:
Sleep clinics routinely ask for one or two weeks of diary before and alongside testing, and it earns its place because it answers questions no single night in a lab can.

Before a sleep study, the diary tells the clinician what your normal actually is. A study night in a lab or with a home kit measures one or two nights of physiology; the diary supplies the context — that you're averaging five and a half hours, or that your bedtime swings by three hours, or that Sunday is always your worst night. It also helps ensure the study is done at a sensible time for your schedule, which matters a great deal for shift workers.

To tell conditions apart. The three big possibilities look similar from the inside and quite different on paper. Insufficient sleep shows normal quality but too few hours. A circadian rhythm disorder shows good sleep at the "wrong" clock times, with a consistent pattern. Insomnia shows long sleep-onset times or long awakenings despite plenty of opportunity. And repeated unexplained awakenings plus daytime sleepiness with normal hours raises the question of a breathing problem — see sleep apnea signs.

To run treatment. Behavioral treatment for insomnia is driven directly by diary numbers — the prescribed time in bed is set from your average sleep time and widened as your efficiency improves. Without a diary there's nothing to set it from. On CPAP therapy, the diary sits next to the machine's usage data: the machine says how many hours it ran, the diary says how you slept and felt, and the pair is what a review appointment actually works from.

Bring the whole thing, not a summary. Your clinician wants to see the spread and the outliers, not just the average.

sections.heading: Paper vs app: an honest comparison
sections.html:
Paper works. This template printed on a sheet by the bed, a pen, and two minutes each morning is a complete, clinically useful sleep diary, and plenty of people have solved their sleep with exactly that. If it's what you'll keep, keep it.

Where paper costs you is everything after the fourteenth morning. Nobody averages fourteen nights of elapsed sleep by hand, and nobody computes sleep efficiency twice. Patterns hide inside columns of times. The sheet is never where you left it. And three months later, when the clinic asks how things are going compared to before, the sheet is gone.

Sleep & CPAP Feeltracker is this template, automated. It's a manual diary rather than an automatic sleep-stage tracker — it doesn't listen to the room or guess your stages, and it doesn't pretend to — which is precisely what a clinical sleep diary is meant to be:

  • Sleep and wake times with elapsed time slept calculated for you, so averages and efficiency don't depend on arithmetic at 7 a.m.
  • Sleep-quality rating, notes, and dream recording — the whole Notes column, searchable, with the caffeine, alcohol and exercise entries you'd otherwise scribble in a margin.
  • CPAP usage logging, if that's part of your picture, in the same history rather than a separate app.
  • Charts and trends over any period — the two-week average, the weekday-versus-weekend gap, and the before-and-after of a change, drawn rather than derived.
  • Export to PDF, XLSX, CSV or JSON — a clean, dated record to hand a clinician, instead of a photograph of a handwritten page.
  • Reminders to log in the morning while it's accurate, widgets for one-tap entry, and Apple Health sync.
  • iCloud sync with no account and no email address, on iPhone, iPad and Mac — plus AI insights over your own history (free, with optional premium) if you want a plain-English read on your own pattern.

Whichever you choose, start tonight rather than on a "normal" week. There's no such thing as a normal week, and the diary you begin today is already two weeks ahead of the one you're waiting to start.

items.question: How long should I keep a sleep diary?
items.answer: **Two consecutive weeks** is the standard, because it captures weekdays and weekends twice and lets a pattern separate itself from a couple of bad nights. One week is the minimum most clinicians will work from; longer is useful when you're tracking the effect of a change.

items.question: What if I don't know exactly when I fell asleep?
items.answer: Estimate — that's what everyone does, and what clinicians expect. Deliberately **don't** watch the clock during the night: checking the time repeatedly makes both your sleep and your diary worse. Fill the row in from your best guess within half an hour of getting up.

items.question: Should I record bad nights?
items.answer: Especially the bad nights. A tidied-up diary is worse than none, because it points your clinician at the wrong problem. If you miss a morning entirely, leave the row blank rather than reconstructing it days later.

items.question: What is sleep efficiency and what's a good number?
items.answer: Time actually asleep divided by time in bed, as a percentage. Above roughly **85%** is generally considered healthy. A much lower figure usually means you're spending more time in bed than you're sleeping — the exact pattern that behavioral treatment for [insomnia](/sleep/insomnia-causes/) is designed to correct.

items.question: Does a sleep diary replace a sleep study?
items.answer: No — they answer different questions and clinics use both. A study measures your breathing, oxygen and brain activity for a night or two; a diary shows your habitual pattern across weeks. If a breathing problem is suspected, only a study can confirm it; see [sleep apnea signs](/sleep/sleep-apnea-signs/).

data.disclaimerText: This article is for general information only and is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. A sleep diary supports, but never replaces, professional assessment — always follow the guidance of your doctor or healthcare provider, and never start, stop, or change a medication on your own. See a doctor promptly if you fall asleep uncontrollably during the day, if daytime sleepiness is affecting your driving, or if someone has seen you stop breathing, gasp, or choke in your sleep.
